[[:db/retract 17592186129525 :question/answer-fields 17592186126649] [:db/retract 17592186129509 :question/answer-fields 17592186126554] {:db/id 17592186129187 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-fdaff75b-e0c6-5e92-b720-ea0f3e9d5336"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129006 :question/problem "Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

![](images/eb/eb8cb887e2c6e273a9a59bdbffeb0e8a2af4f8dcf5cc376ba4318128201ef936.svg)" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

![](images/92/928c9f7761e597884525a92388346c486c4e0df9c2c942cf31ad87164676613e.svg)

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x=(u+v)^3$ and $y=(u-v)^2.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =3(u+v)^{2} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =3(u+v)^{2} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2(u-v) & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2(u-v)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3(u+v)^{2} & 3(u+v)^{2} \\ 2(u-v) & -2(u-v)\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(u+v)^{2}\cdot (-2(u-v))-3(u+v)^{2}\cdot 2(u-v) \\  & =-12(u+v)^{2}(u-v).\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128838 :question/problem "For the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

![](images/7f/7fc9eb28594744f04c1934d10b7e9751c9f9855897f4cc4da05b8a5e82a93f3d.svg)

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where ![](images/5e/5e056d63a91b0f4ae7dcb1c076764b862b0321b47c6e586cc91acd9e01dd36c8.svg)" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

![](images/37/370aba8042cc3dbd6c5c9dc15751e50dd8fe7be36d0cb220966da075bf9e2e43.svg)

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v) = 2v\cos{u}$ and $y(u,v) = v\sin{u}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-2v\operatorname{sin}⁡u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =v\operatorname{cos}⁡u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2v\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\ v\operatorname{cos}⁡u & \operatorname{sin}⁡u\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2v\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡u-2\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot v\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\  & =-2v({sin}^{2}⁡u+{cos}^{2}⁡u) \\  & =-2v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when ![](images/1c/1ca433e68fd2a57e9bd9666b76c0577fd84621eededde3a50d03a49723b21739.svg) the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
\left.\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}\right|_{(0,-1)} = -2(-1) = 2.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128860 :question/problem "Consider a small rectangle $\Delta$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(-1,2)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta{A}.$ Find an approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by
![](images/ff/ff668919204d7ccd57c1711fed961ca73562d47cc6f100511b06fe54a5ea212d.svg)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128861 :question/problem "Sketch the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ given by 
![](images/57/57874e6e685ee9fb1a2b527fe046696aa983b04d22751c72d8a76783b349ca18.svg)
is (locally) orientation-reversing." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}  <    0
$$

We have

![](images/45/4595adcbeb5ee3dc0bbe1258536e9b0e3e2fc81d5720a3394029df814f55f949.svg)

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{v} & u{e}^{v} \\ 2u & -2v\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{v}\cdot (-2v)-u{e}^{v}\cdot 2u \\  & =-2{e}^{v}({u}^{2}+v).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{v}({u}^{2}+v) & <0 \\ {u}^{2}+v & >0 \\ v & >-{u}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v=-u^2
$$

defines a downward-opening parabola, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing must be the following:

![](images/2b/2b6128c5a1737e3ad1fd82f91f5ccd320421ad3472ae8152440034ecea10d364.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-fdaff75b-e0c6-5e92-b720-ea0f3e9d5336" :question/id #uuid "fdaff75b-e0c6-5e92-b720-ea0f3e9d5336" :question/math-academy-id "q-81263" :question/problem "Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T([\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{ln}⁡v \\ {u}^{2}{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Here, we have $x=u\operatorname{ln}⁡v$ and $y={u}^{2}{v}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\frac{u}{v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u{v}^{2} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2{u}^{2}v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡v & \frac{u}{v} \\ 2u{v}^{2} & 2{u}^{2}v\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡v\cdot 2{u}^{2}v-\frac{u}{v}\cdot 2u{v}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}v(\operatorname{ln}⁡v-1).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-07041bd7-da85-5245-8203-4f70786b0ce5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-07041bd7-da85-5245-8203-4f70786b0ce5" :answer-field/id #uuid "07041bd7-da85-5245-8203-4f70786b0ce5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3ee2cdb4-9a34-5a8b-a223-2ea4a089aa37" :answer-field/choices ["answer-97d54cc4-bb7e-5809-af16-75ed6fdc3a2d" "answer-962f026a-a6e1-5e0c-8e81-b3f195d58e6c" "answer-3ee2cdb4-9a34-5a8b-a223-2ea4a089aa37" "answer-4c763f52-9b23-5041-b90c-5411e27f7574" "answer-fc2ceb4d-c670-5d4a-ba41-be274f566d61"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-97d54cc4-bb7e-5809-af16-75ed6fdc3a2d" :answer/id #uuid "97d54cc4-bb7e-5809-af16-75ed6fdc3a2d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2uv(\operatorname{ln}⁡v-v)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-962f026a-a6e1-5e0c-8e81-b3f195d58e6c" :answer/id #uuid "962f026a-a6e1-5e0c-8e81-b3f195d58e6c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{u}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡v-v)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3ee2cdb4-9a34-5a8b-a223-2ea4a089aa37" :answer/id #uuid "3ee2cdb4-9a34-5a8b-a223-2ea4a089aa37" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{u}^{2}v(\operatorname{ln}⁡v-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4c763f52-9b23-5041-b90c-5411e27f7574" :answer/id #uuid "4c763f52-9b23-5041-b90c-5411e27f7574" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4uv(\operatorname{ln}⁡v-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fc2ceb4d-c670-5d4a-ba41-be274f566d61" :answer/id #uuid "fc2ceb4d-c670-5d4a-ba41-be274f566d61" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4{u}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡v-v)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130392 :tutorial/content "We have explored linear and affine transformations in the plane. We'll now begin to explore nonlinear transformations of plane regions. 

Let  $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be a **transformation** on an open set $U\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ We write
![](images/11/1137221ffc72c194aba941eaee899cc0a4134a92e92e86cfa65c88acd5f702ec.svg) 

Recall that, under this notation, 

- ![](images/0d/0decb326ae66f97fb75a8df874479061fb1557b0437ca8ea1e7c5ed645db4b19.svg) represents vectors belonging to the input space (i.e., the $uv$-plane), and

- ![](images/09/091b7a3ddf6ad7dc35360e728c2946481b3a17f60525d09676eb469ebd518a4d.svg) represents vectors belonging to the output space (i.e., the $xy$-plane).

For example, consider the following transformation:

![](images/23/239781240f2def3a5adf5331f36fa6dbdd3657ab431195c30cf3ede49d2ef3e2.svg) 

Geometrically, this transformation maps the rectangular region in the $uv$-plane below to a circular sector in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/dc/dcc80fe1271d560e9f958eba9454761d56f936567dc439853bc4181cccc3f76f.png)

We'll explore how to compute the image of a nonlinear transformation in future lessons. But for now, it is sufficient to know that 

- $\mathbf T$ takes points (or vectors) from the $uv$-plane as input and maps them to points (vectors) in the $xy$-plane, and

- rectangular regions in the $uv$-plane are mapped to regions in the $xy$-plane that are not necessarily parallelograms." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130460 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation given by

![](images/f9/f9a1c3375eed570284c4e001f119f21901f4493a0b851919b92b678a74187444.svg) 

We'll assume that $\mathbf T$ is a $\boldsymbol{C}^1$ **transformation**, which means that  $x$ and $y$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set $U$ contained in $\Bbb R^2.$ 

The **Jacobian determinant** of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|=\frac{∂x}{∂u}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂v}-\frac{∂x}{∂v}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂u}\end{aligned}
$$

  

We sometimes refer to the Jacobian determinant simply as the **Jacobian.**

Let's compute the Jacobian determinant of the following transformation:

![](images/b4/b433bcafea1c84c67f2fb65ac8343a4d8401ce6d4e745f6d464b010a4258164a.svg) 

To compute the Jacobian determinant of this function, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-(-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =u{cos}^{2}⁡v+u{sin}^{2}⁡v \\  & =u({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & =u.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We'll spend some time discussing the meaning behind the Jacobian shortly. But for now, let's get some practice at computing it." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130461 :tutorial/content "To understand what the Jacobian describes, we recall our knowledge of affine transformations.

Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\Bbb R^2 \to \Bbb R^2,$ defined by the matrix equation 

$$
\mathbf x = T\mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf u, \mathbf b,$ and $\mathbf x$ are vectors from $\mathbb R^2,$ and $T$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix. 

For an affine transformation, the determinant of $T$ gives us the following information:

- The *area scale factor* of the transformation:

If a rectangle in the $uv$-plane has area $A,$ its image in the $xy$-plane is a parallelogram of area $|\det(T)|\cdot A.$

![](images/04/04f36d98bf7589d1faadeffee0812590337fd36d8bb44f5abe1920948dee5bb0.png)

- Whether the transformation is *orientation-preserving* or *orientation-reversing:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) > 0,$ the transformation is orientation-preserving.

![](images/49/496a49ee541eab31f69f9c571e450547b0c6942b100bc8e24fbd927dd43e4d33.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) < 0,$ the transformation is orientation-reversing.

![](images/21/211369d6f3fc70bcf7cf40f3270c24c245d306247efc429cb85589e42c19ee07.png)

- Whether the transformation is *invertible* or *non-invertible:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) \neq 0,$ the transformation is invertible.

![](images/e4/e4b840ad5a3efa082ac4056d1d9b7c03d2e3e11e016e053df055dbb2b39f0d1f.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) = 0,$ the transformation is non-invertible. In such cases, a rectangle in the $uv$-plane collapses to either a line segment or point in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/9a/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)

![](images/98/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)

Affine transformations are special because these properties are *global*. In other words, they apply *everywhere* in the plane. So, for example, if $\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130462 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.

The critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. 

To understand what this means, suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where
![](images/d0/d0149013f12e5cdad31611d4c64489c0aaf6049707e9eed22202ae70d2d8a38a.svg) 

and we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$

For ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$

$$
J(u_0,v_0) = \left.\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}
$$

Let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$

![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)

It's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be *approximated* by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson). 

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:

- The *local* area scale factor of $\mathbf T$. 

Suppose the length and width of our rectangle are $\delta u$ and $\delta v,$ so its area is $\delta A = \delta u\delta v.$ Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the $xy$-plane has an area equal to $\left|J(u_0,v_0)\right| \cdot \delta A.$

![](images/be/be1771ebb041c418c58d7d5615510e2fcacfeaf3677fbace739498ef1998ef11.png)

Note the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced $\det(T)$ with the Jacobian).

- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0)> 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.

![](images/8c/8c649fdd526a831fb990393b292fb4582dad14c2391d129e9ed59792ebb8ac31.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)<  0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

![](images/ae/ae5a3d0a42e1c4b9f692994b89815382a30cdf3e676bbd9844258ad2a6961608.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0)\neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

![](images/33/33ca98206a347e13aa8ec179a52dd755008d9a7d74882391e0c3f2344f6f6641.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

![](images/3d/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)

![](images/65/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)

Points $(u_0,v_0)$ such that $J(u_0,v_0)=0$ are called **critical points.** Critical points are very important. We'll discuss these in more detail in future lessons.

We again stress that the Jacobian describes *local* properties, that is, local to the point $(u_0,v_0).$ The effect of a nonlinear transformation on an object varies as we move around the $uv$-plane, so its local properties also vary. So, for example, if a transformation is orientation-preserving at one point, it does *not* mean it's orientation-preserving everywhere!" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129344 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$

$$

is (locally) orientation-reversing." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

We have

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{v} & u{e}^{v} \\ 2u & -2v\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{v}\cdot (-2v)-u{e}^{v}\cdot 2u \\  & =-2{e}^{v}({u}^{2}+v).\end{aligned}

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{v}({u}^{2}+v) & <0 \\ {u}^{2}+v & >0 \\ v & >-{u}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$

$$

defines a downward-opening parabola, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing must be the following:

![](images/2b/2b6128c5a1737e3ad1fd82f91f5ccd320421ad3472ae8152440034ecea10d364.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-fdaff75b-e0c6-5e92-b720-ea0f3e9d5336" :question/id #uuid "fdaff75b-e0c6-5e92-b720-ea0f3e9d5336" :question/math-academy-id "q-81263" :question/problem "Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T([\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{ln}⁡v \\ {u}^{2}{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Here, we have $x=u\operatorname{ln}⁡v$ and $y={u}^{2}{v}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\frac{u}{v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u{v}^{2} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2{u}^{2}v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡v & \frac{u}{v} \\ 2u{v}^{2} & 2{u}^{2}v\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡v\cdot 2{u}^{2}v-\frac{u}{v}\cdot 2u{v}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}v(\operatorname{ln}⁡v-1).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-07041bd7-da85-5245-8203-4f70786b0ce5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-07041bd7-da85-5245-8203-4f70786b0ce5" :answer-field/id #uuid "07041bd7-da85-5245-8203-4f70786b0ce5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3ee2cdb4-9a34-5a8b-a223-2ea4a089aa37" :answer-field/choices ["answer-97d54cc4-bb7e-5809-af16-75ed6fdc3a2d" "answer-962f026a-a6e1-5e0c-8e81-b3f195d58e6c" "answer-3ee2cdb4-9a34-5a8b-a223-2ea4a089aa37" "answer-4c763f52-9b23-5041-b90c-5411e27f7574" "answer-fc2ceb4d-c670-5d4a-ba41-be274f566d61"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-97d54cc4-bb7e-5809-af16-75ed6fdc3a2d" :answer/id #uuid "97d54cc4-bb7e-5809-af16-75ed6fdc3a2d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2uv(\operatorname{ln}⁡v-v)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-962f026a-a6e1-5e0c-8e81-b3f195d58e6c" :answer/id #uuid "962f026a-a6e1-5e0c-8e81-b3f195d58e6c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{u}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡v-v)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3ee2cdb4-9a34-5a8b-a223-2ea4a089aa37" :answer/id #uuid "3ee2cdb4-9a34-5a8b-a223-2ea4a089aa37" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{u}^{2}v(\operatorname{ln}⁡v-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4c763f52-9b23-5041-b90c-5411e27f7574" :answer/id #uuid "4c763f52-9b23-5041-b90c-5411e27f7574" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4uv(\operatorname{ln}⁡v-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fc2ceb4d-c670-5d4a-ba41-be274f566d61" :answer/id #uuid "fc2ceb4d-c670-5d4a-ba41-be274f566d61" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4{u}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡v-v)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130392 :tutorial/content "We have explored linear and affine transformations in the plane. We'll now begin to explore nonlinear transformations of plane regions. 

Let  $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be a **transformation** on an open set $U\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ We write
![](images/11/1137221ffc72c194aba941eaee899cc0a4134a92e92e86cfa65c88acd5f702ec.svg) 

Recall that, under this notation, 

- ![](images/0d/0decb326ae66f97fb75a8df874479061fb1557b0437ca8ea1e7c5ed645db4b19.svg) represents vectors belonging to the input space (i.e., the $uv$-plane), and

- ![](images/09/091b7a3ddf6ad7dc35360e728c2946481b3a17f60525d09676eb469ebd518a4d.svg) represents vectors belonging to the output space (i.e., the $xy$-plane).

For example, consider the following transformation:

![](images/23/239781240f2def3a5adf5331f36fa6dbdd3657ab431195c30cf3ede49d2ef3e2.svg) 

Geometrically, this transformation maps the rectangular region in the $uv$-plane below to a circular sector in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/dc/dcc80fe1271d560e9f958eba9454761d56f936567dc439853bc4181cccc3f76f.png)

We'll explore how to compute the image of a nonlinear transformation in future lessons. But for now, it is sufficient to know that 

- $\mathbf T$ takes points (or vectors) from the $uv$-plane as input and maps them to points (vectors) in the $xy$-plane, and

- rectangular regions in the $uv$-plane are mapped to regions in the $xy$-plane that are not necessarily parallelograms." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130460 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation given by

![](images/f9/f9a1c3375eed570284c4e001f119f21901f4493a0b851919b92b678a74187444.svg) 

We'll assume that $\mathbf T$ is a $\boldsymbol{C}^1$ **transformation**, which means that  $x$ and $y$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set $U$ contained in $\Bbb R^2.$ 

The **Jacobian determinant** of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|=\frac{∂x}{∂u}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂v}-\frac{∂x}{∂v}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂u}\end{aligned}
$$

  

We sometimes refer to the Jacobian determinant simply as the **Jacobian.**

Let's compute the Jacobian determinant of the following transformation:

![](images/b4/b433bcafea1c84c67f2fb65ac8343a4d8401ce6d4e745f6d464b010a4258164a.svg) 

To compute the Jacobian determinant of this function, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-(-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =u{cos}^{2}⁡v+u{sin}^{2}⁡v \\  & =u({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & =u.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We'll spend some time discussing the meaning behind the Jacobian shortly. But for now, let's get some practice at computing it." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130461 :tutorial/content "To understand what the Jacobian describes, we recall our knowledge of affine transformations.

Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\Bbb R^2 \to \Bbb R^2,$ defined by the matrix equation 

$$
\mathbf x = T\mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf u, \mathbf b,$ and $\mathbf x$ are vectors from $\mathbb R^2,$ and $T$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix. 

For an affine transformation, the determinant of $T$ gives us the following information:

- The *area scale factor* of the transformation:

If a rectangle in the $uv$-plane has area $A,$ its image in the $xy$-plane is a parallelogram of area $|\det(T)|\cdot A.$

![](images/04/04f36d98bf7589d1faadeffee0812590337fd36d8bb44f5abe1920948dee5bb0.png)

- Whether the transformation is *orientation-preserving* or *orientation-reversing:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) > 0,$ the transformation is orientation-preserving.

![](images/49/496a49ee541eab31f69f9c571e450547b0c6942b100bc8e24fbd927dd43e4d33.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) < 0,$ the transformation is orientation-reversing.

![](images/21/211369d6f3fc70bcf7cf40f3270c24c245d306247efc429cb85589e42c19ee07.png)

- Whether the transformation is *invertible* or *non-invertible:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) \neq 0,$ the transformation is invertible.

![](images/e4/e4b840ad5a3efa082ac4056d1d9b7c03d2e3e11e016e053df055dbb2b39f0d1f.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) = 0,$ the transformation is non-invertible. In such cases, a rectangle in the $uv$-plane collapses to either a line segment or point in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/9a/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)

![](images/98/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)

Affine transformations are special because these properties are *global*. In other words, they apply *everywhere* in the plane. So, for example, if $\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130462 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.

The critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. 

To understand what this means, suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where
![](images/d0/d0149013f12e5cdad31611d4c64489c0aaf6049707e9eed22202ae70d2d8a38a.svg) 

and we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$

For ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$

$$
J(u_0,v_0) = \left.\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}
$$

Let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$

![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)

It's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be *approximated* by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson). 

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:

- The *local* area scale factor of $\mathbf T$. 

Suppose the length and width of our rectangle are $\delta u$ and $\delta v,$ so its area is $\delta A = \delta u\delta v.$ Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the $xy$-plane has an area equal to $\left|J(u_0,v_0)\right| \cdot \delta A.$

![](images/be/be1771ebb041c418c58d7d5615510e2fcacfeaf3677fbace739498ef1998ef11.png)

Note the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced $\det(T)$ with the Jacobian).

- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0)> 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.

![](images/8c/8c649fdd526a831fb990393b292fb4582dad14c2391d129e9ed59792ebb8ac31.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)<  0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

![](images/ae/ae5a3d0a42e1c4b9f692994b89815382a30cdf3e676bbd9844258ad2a6961608.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0)\neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

![](images/33/33ca98206a347e13aa8ec179a52dd755008d9a7d74882391e0c3f2344f6f6641.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

![](images/3d/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)

![](images/65/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)

Points $(u_0,v_0)$ such that $J(u_0,v_0)=0$ are called **critical points.** Critical points are very important. We'll discuss these in more detail in future lessons.

We again stress that the Jacobian describes *local* properties, that is, local to the point $(u_0,v_0).$ The effect of a nonlinear transformation on an object varies as we move around the $uv$-plane, so its local properties also vary. So, for example, if a transformation is orientation-preserving at one point, it does *not* mean it's orientation-preserving everywhere!" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129344 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186129006 :question/problem "Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

$$

We'll assume that $\mathbf T$ is a $\boldsymbol{C}^1$ **transformation**, which means that $x$ and $y$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set $U$ contained in $\Bbb R^2.$

The **Jacobian determinant** of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is defined as

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|=\frac{∂x}{∂u}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂v}-\frac{∂x}{∂v}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂u}\end{aligned}$$

We sometimes refer to the Jacobian determinant simply as the **Jacobian.**

Let's compute the Jacobian determinant of the following transformation:

$$[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] = \mathbf{T}\left( [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] \right) = [\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{cos}v \\ u\operatorname{sin}v\end{aligned}]$$

To compute the Jacobian determinant of this function, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}v\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}v & -u\operatorname{sin}v \\ \operatorname{sin}v & u\operatorname{cos}v\end{aligned}| \\ & =\operatorname{cos}v\cdot (u\operatorname{cos}v)-(-u\operatorname{sin}v)\cdot \operatorname{sin}v \\ & =u{cos}^{2}v+u{sin}^{2}v \\ & =u({cos}^{2}v+{sin}^{2}v) \\ & =u.\end{aligned}$$

We'll spend some time discussing the meaning behind the Jacobian shortly. But for now, let's get some practice at computing it."] [17592186130461 :tutorial/content "To understand what the Jacobian describes, we recall our knowledge of affine transformations.

Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\Bbb R^2 \to \Bbb R^2,$ defined by the matrix equation

$$\mathbf x = T\mathbf u + \mathbf b,$$

where $\mathbf u, \mathbf b,$ and $\mathbf x$ are vectors from $\mathbb R^2,$ and $T$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

For an affine transformation, the determinant of $T$ gives us the following information:

- The *area scale factor* of the transformation:

If a rectangle in the $uv$-plane has area $A,$ its image in the $xy$-plane is a parallelogram of area $|\det(T)|\cdot A.$

![](images/04/04f36d98bf7589d1faadeffee0812590337fd36d8bb44f5abe1920948dee5bb0.png)
- Whether the transformation is *orientation-preserving* or *orientation-reversing:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) > 0,$ the transformation is orientation-preserving.

![](images/49/496a49ee541eab31f69f9c571e450547b0c6942b100bc8e24fbd927dd43e4d33.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) < 0,$ the transformation is orientation-reversing.

![](images/21/211369d6f3fc70bcf7cf40f3270c24c245d306247efc429cb85589e42c19ee07.png)

- Whether the transformation is *invertible* or *non-invertible:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) \neq 0,$ the transformation is invertible.

![](images/e4/e4b840ad5a3efa082ac4056d1d9b7c03d2e3e11e016e053df055dbb2b39f0d1f.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) = 0,$ the transformation is non-invertible. In such cases, a rectangle in the $uv$-plane collapses to either a line segment or point in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/9a/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)

![](images/98/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)

Affine transformations are special because these properties are *global*. In other words, they apply *everywhere* in the plane. So, for example, if $\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage."] [17592186130462 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.

The critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones.

To understand what this means, suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where $$\mathbf{T}: [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] \longrightarrow [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]$$

and we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$

For ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$

$$J(u_0,v_0) = \left.\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}$$

Let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$

![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)

It's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be *approximated* by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson).

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:

- The *local* area scale factor of $\mathbf T$.

Suppose the length and width of our rectangle are $\delta u$ and $\delta v,$ so its area is $\delta A = \delta u\delta v.$ Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the $xy$-plane has an area equal to $\left|J(u_0,v_0)\right| \cdot \delta A.$

![](images/be/be1771ebb041c418c58d7d5615510e2fcacfeaf3677fbace739498ef1998ef11.png)

Note the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced $\det(T)$ with the Jacobian).
- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0)> 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.

![](images/8c/8c649fdd526a831fb990393b292fb4582dad14c2391d129e9ed59792ebb8ac31.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)< 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

![](images/ae/ae5a3d0a42e1c4b9f692994b89815382a30cdf3e676bbd9844258ad2a6961608.png)
- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0)\neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

![](images/33/33ca98206a347e13aa8ec179a52dd755008d9a7d74882391e0c3f2344f6f6641.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

![](images/3d/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)

![](images/65/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)

Points $(u_0,v_0)$ such that $J(u_0,v_0)=0$ are called **critical points.** Critical points are very important. We'll discuss these in more detail in future lessons.

We again stress that the Jacobian describes *local* properties, that is, local to the point $(u_0,v_0).$ The effect of a nonlinear transformation on an object varies as we move around the $uv$-plane, so its local properties also vary. So, for example, if a transformation is orientation-preserving at one point, it does *not* mean it's orientation-preserving everywhere!"]]}

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)$ and $y=4u+6v.$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =4 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \,\text{ }4\, & \,\text{ }6\end{aligned}| \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\cdot 6-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v))\cdot 4 \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351278 :question/id #uuid "3a033a41-4f6f-52b1-9278-922a7269908f" :question/math-academy-id "q-81252" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129187 :knowledge-point/id #uuid $$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=2u\operatorname{cos}⁡v$ and $y(u,v)=3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-2u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡v & -2u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot 3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-(-2u\operatorname{sin}⁡v)\cdot 3\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =6u({cos}^{2}⁡v+{cos}^{2}⁡v) \\  & =6u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(1,2)}=6(1)=6.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129508 :question/id #uuid "fa6e908a-36ba-5f5c-b35a-6753290d1954" :question/math-academy-id "q-160394"} {:db/id 17592186278288 :question/id #uuid "2b1f8f7b-fd82-5c84-a276-7fa2fd9b071a" :question/math-academy-id "q-160383" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27184dd5-9306-5151-ba71-71c0184555b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186275833} {:answer/id #uuid "921684d8-1a85-53da-b8a7-23bd356d4d8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186276799} {:answer/id #uuid "a6b6ecd9-7efa-5fbf-99f4-87cf3cf2fc2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186276980} {:answer/id #uuid "a9f4d180-9148-56f8-af89-c87393729376" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186277007} {:answer/id #uuid "bc4ef6cf-c02f-531a-934f-84c5afac9290" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186277153}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186276799} :answer-field/id #uuid "3f823688-c59b-5a64-9e51-9b7c368087e1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186277821}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "For the transformation $T,$ defined as

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x=uv$ and $y=\frac{v}{u}.$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-\frac{v}{{u}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v & u \\ -\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}\, & \frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}| \\  & =v\cdot \frac{1}{u}\text{ }-u\cdot (-\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{2v}{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-2,3)}=\frac{2(3)}{-2}=-3.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278291 :question/id #uuid "2443aa6d-e746-5170-93b3-e30684a9a33b" :question/math-academy-id "q-160402"} {:db/id 17592186278296 :question/id #uuid "861c1236-2662-5b7d-b150-03b6774d0f17" :question/math-academy-id "q-160427" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129263 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ab643519-92a4-5ccf-b826-fb2a68b36534" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Jacobian Determinant"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a030248-80e5-5392-828d-2bf5b0f34c56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186275988} {:answer/id #uuid "46441063-cd17-57f8-93da-47999b8389f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-8" :db/id 17592186276099} {:answer/id #uuid "4d076db5-f0b8-5a55-b9f9-a751427c3ef4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "14" :db/id 17592186276158} {:answer/id #uuid "8d6588ee-c55c-5f42-9ca1-f5f8f0e473ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186276758} {:answer/id #uuid "dc0b5777-e3d4-5733-95a0-9024964404d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186277404}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "3a030248-80e5-5392-828d-2bf5b0f34c56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186275988} :answer-field/id #uuid "ade1226d-3be4-5422-9ead-d085939320b3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186278025}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 2v \\ 2u & -2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-2v)-2v\cdot 2u \\  & =-4uv-4uv \\  & =-8uv.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-2,1)}=-8(-2)(1)=16.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278297 :question/id #uuid "19415143-780a-5182-8164-c1af6838225c" :question/math-academy-id "q-160428" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129263 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ab643519-92a4-5ccf-b826-fb2a68b36534" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Jacobian Determinant"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7338df5d-9ede-525b-86f7-9575217f0621" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186276521} {:answer/id #uuid "9194b3db-7eb6-5b12-82d1-c39ced725329" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186276796} {:answer/id #uuid "9f339d05-8ec4-52fc-929d-9e259b65d946" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186276908} {:answer/id #uuid "ae707e98-98f8-52a3-8963-4e1ec7a26492" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186277042} {:answer/id #uuid "e115090f-5258-55ab-a7de-95ef1c7a3b91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186277445}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "7338df5d-9ede-525b-86f7-9575217f0621" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186276521} :answer-field/id #uuid "cc930da6-f008-59fd-875c-d797cf29d182" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186278084}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$

$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}

Here, we have $x(u,v)=\frac{{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}}{2}$ and $y(u,v)=uv.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\end{aligned}

$$

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-1,-2)}=(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}=5.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278298 :question/id #uuid "876a5d15-9cbd-5150-8246-c71dbabaa45c" :question/math-academy-id "q-160431" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129263 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ab643519-92a4-5ccf-b826-fb2a68b36534" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Jacobian Determinant"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "09e0e11f-ca64-573d-aa4a-39c0085748ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186275562} {:answer/id #uuid "2571ec42-1410-5512-abb4-5d9f33e67cf4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186275817} {:answer/id #uuid "6056f233-baaf-59fc-ab26-47501271c259" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186276339} {:answer/id #uuid "e97346e5-01ac-55ce-b840-edd902ee3c65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186277517} {:answer/id #uuid "fa81b135-dfdc-52eb-85bc-1dd61c22d3d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186277669}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "e97346e5-01ac-55ce-b840-edd902ee3c65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186277517} :answer-field/id #uuid "946d36e5-48fa-5671-b5c2-6b9df0953fbc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186277988}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "For the transformation $T,$ defined as

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

$$

$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={v}^{2}+uv$ and $y(u,v)=v-u.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v+u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$

$$

by

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡u & -2v \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\cdot 1-1\cdot (-2v) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u+2v \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(0,3)} & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡u+2v)\,{|}_{u=0\,v=3} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡0+2(3) \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|6|\cdot \delta A \\  & =6\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281371 :question/id #uuid "4a48d509-ce9f-57c3-ab71-29eb65410f8f" :question/math-academy-id "q-161885" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129282 :knowledge-point/id #uuid $$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\ 3{u}^{2} & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u+v}\cdot 1-3{u}^{2}\cdot {e}^{u+v} \\  & ={e}^{u+v}(1-3{u}^{2}) \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-2,2)} & ={e}^{u+v}(1-3{u}^{2})\,{|}_{u=-2\,v=2} \\  & ={e}^{-2+2}(1-3(-2)^{2}) \\  & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

is (locally) orientation-preserving?" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving at the points where the Jacobian determinant is positive:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}>0.
$$

We have

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-v \\ 4u-{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & -1 \\ 4 & -2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-2v)-4\cdot (-1) \\  & =-4uv+4.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4uv+4 & >0 \\ -4uv & >-4 \\ uv & <1\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives the solution $v<\frac{1}{u}$ for $u>0$ and $v>\frac{1}{u}$ for $u<0.$

Notice that the equation 

$$
v=\frac{1}{u}
$$

defines a hyperbola, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,-1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving must be the following:

T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} \\ -uv\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\ -v & -u\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u+v}\cdot (-u)-(-v)\cdot {e}^{u+v} \\  & ={e}^{u+v}(v-u).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v}(v-u) & >0 \\ v-u & >0 \\ v & >u\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v=u
$$

defines a straight line, and the coordinates of, say, $(2,3)$ satisfy the inequality.

We'll now begin to explore nonlinear transformations of plane regions.

Let $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be a **transformation** on an open set $U\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ We write $$\mathbf{T}: [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] \longrightarrow [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}].$$

Recall that, under this notation,

- $\mathbf u = [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]$ represents vectors belonging to the input space (i.e., the $uv$-plane), and
- $\mathbf x = [\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]$ represents vectors belonging to the output space (i.e., the $xy$-plane).

For example, consider the following transformation:

$$[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] = \mathbf{T}\left( [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] \right) = [\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{cos}v \\ u\operatorname{sin}v\end{aligned}]$$

Geometrically, this transformation maps the rectangular region in the $uv$-plane below to a circular sector in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/dc/dcc80fe1271d560e9f958eba9454761d56f936567dc439853bc4181cccc3f76f.png)

We'll explore how to compute the image of a nonlinear transformation in future lessons. But for now, it is sufficient to know that

- $\mathbf T$ takes points (or vectors) from the $uv$-plane as input and maps them to points (vectors) in the $xy$-plane, and
- rectangular regions in the $uv$-plane are mapped to regions in the $xy$-plane that are not necessarily parallelograms." :tutorial/id #uuid "c831da3f-8fff-5c5b-8be5-f3602a7303ba" {:db/id 17592186130226}} {:db/id 17592186130225 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130460 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation given by

$$\mathbf{T}: [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] \longrightarrow [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}].$$

We'll assume that $\mathbf T$ is a $\boldsymbol{C}^1$ **transformation**, which means that $x$ and $y$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set $U$ contained in $\Bbb R^2.$

The **Jacobian determinant** of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is defined as

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|=\frac{∂x}{∂u}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂v}-\frac{∂x}{∂v}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂u}\end{aligned}$$

We sometimes refer to the Jacobian determinant simply as the **Jacobian.**

Let's compute the Jacobian determinant of the following transformation:

$$[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] = \mathbf{T}\left( [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] \right) = [\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{cos}v \\ u\operatorname{sin}v\end{aligned}]$$

To compute the Jacobian determinant of this function, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}v\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}v & -u\operatorname{sin}v \\ \operatorname{sin}v & u\operatorname{cos}v\end{aligned}| \\ & =\operatorname{cos}v\cdot (u\operatorname{cos}v)-(-u\operatorname{sin}v)\cdot \operatorname{sin}v \\ & =u{cos}^{2}v+u{sin}^{2}v \\ & =u({cos}^{2}v+{sin}^{2}v) \\ & =u.\end{aligned}$$

We'll spend some time discussing the meaning behind the Jacobian shortly. But for now, let's get some practice at computing it." :tutorial/id #uuid "f0ea7366-d3d6-5645-99d8-72f7febb8d19" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7668 :tutorial/title "The Jacobian Determinant"} :step/id #uuid "eadcf9f2-f662-5ba3-8bbc-b9166dfa1142" :step/math-academy-id 44550 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130065}} {:db/id 17592186130226 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130461 :tutorial/content "To understand what the Jacobian describes, we recall our knowledge of affine transformations.

Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\Bbb R^2 \to \Bbb R^2,$ defined by the matrix equation

$$\mathbf x = T\mathbf u + \mathbf b,$$

where $\mathbf u, \mathbf b,$ and $\mathbf x$ are vectors from $\mathbb R^2,$ and $T$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

For an affine transformation, the determinant of $T$ gives us the following information:

- The *area scale factor* of the transformation:

If a rectangle in the $uv$-plane has area $A,$ its image in the $xy$-plane is a parallelogram of area $|\det(T)|\cdot A.$

![](images/04/04f36d98bf7589d1faadeffee0812590337fd36d8bb44f5abe1920948dee5bb0.png)
- Whether the transformation is *orientation-preserving* or *orientation-reversing:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) > 0,$ the transformation is orientation-preserving.

![](images/49/496a49ee541eab31f69f9c571e450547b0c6942b100bc8e24fbd927dd43e4d33.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) < 0,$ the transformation is orientation-reversing.

![](images/21/211369d6f3fc70bcf7cf40f3270c24c245d306247efc429cb85589e42c19ee07.png)

- Whether the transformation is *invertible* or *non-invertible:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) \neq 0,$ the transformation is invertible.

![](images/e4/e4b840ad5a3efa082ac4056d1d9b7c03d2e3e11e016e053df055dbb2b39f0d1f.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) = 0,$ the transformation is non-invertible. In such cases, a rectangle in the $uv$-plane collapses to either a line segment or point in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/9a/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)

![](images/98/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)

Affine transformations are special because these properties are *global*. In other words, they apply *everywhere* in the plane. So, for example, if $\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage." :tutorial/id #uuid "4dcb1ce1-bfad-524c-a89a-a589532a1067" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7672 :tutorial/title "A Review of Affine Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "c956f456-bd29-5cf7-83bd-de9b757b718f" :step/math-academy-id 44557 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130227}} {:db/id 17592186130227 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130462 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.

The critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones.

To understand what this means, suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where $$\mathbf{T}: [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] \longrightarrow [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]$$

and we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$

For ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$

$$J(u_0,v_0) = \left.\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}$$

Let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$

![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)

It's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be *approximated* by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson).

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:

- The *local* area scale factor of $\mathbf T$.

Suppose the length and width of our rectangle are $\delta u$ and $\delta v,$ so its area is $\delta A = \delta u\delta v.$ Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the $xy$-plane has an area equal to $\left|J(u_0,v_0)\right| \cdot \delta A.$

![](images/be/be1771ebb041c418c58d7d5615510e2fcacfeaf3677fbace739498ef1998ef11.png)

Note the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced $\det(T)$ with the Jacobian).
- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0)> 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.

![](images/8c/8c649fdd526a831fb990393b292fb4582dad14c2391d129e9ed59792ebb8ac31.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)< 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

![](images/ae/ae5a3d0a42e1c4b9f692994b89815382a30cdf3e676bbd9844258ad2a6961608.png)
- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0)\neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

![](images/33/33ca98206a347e13aa8ec179a52dd755008d9a7d74882391e0c3f2344f6f6641.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

![](images/3d/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)

![](images/65/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)

Points $(u_0,v_0)$ such that $J(u_0,v_0)=0$ are called **critical points.** Critical points are very important. We'll discuss these in more detail in future lessons.

We again stress that the Jacobian describes *local* properties, that is, local to the point $(u_0,v_0).$ The effect of a nonlinear transformation on an object varies as we move around the $uv$-plane, so its local properties also vary. So, for example, if a transformation is orientation-preserving at one point, it does *not* mean it's orientation-preserving everywhere!" :tutorial/id #uuid "3f6a2c63-d9fc-533c-8c4b-fd822216f0f1" ![](images/9a/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)

![](images/98/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)

Affine transformations are special because these properties are *global*. In other words, they apply *everywhere* in the plane. So, for example, if $\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage." :tutorial/id #uuid "4dcb1ce1-bfad-524c-a89a-a589532a1067" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7672 :tutorial/title "A Review of Affine Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "c956f456-bd29-5cf7-83bd-de9b757b718f" :step/math-academy-id 44557 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130227}} {:db/id 17592186130460 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation given by

$$\mathbf{T}: [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] \longrightarrow [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}].$$

We'll assume that $\mathbf T$ is a $\boldsymbol{C}^1$ **transformation**, which means that $x$ and $y$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set $U$ contained in $\Bbb R^2.$

The **Jacobian determinant** of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is defined as

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|=\frac{∂x}{∂u}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂v}-\frac{∂x}{∂v}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂u}\end{aligned}$$

We sometimes refer to the Jacobian determinant simply as the **Jacobian.**

Let's compute the Jacobian determinant of the following transformation:

$$[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] = \mathbf{T}\left( [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] \right) = [\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{cos}v \\ u\operatorname{sin}v\end{aligned}]$$

To compute the Jacobian determinant of this function, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}v\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}v & -u\operatorname{sin}v \\ \operatorname{sin}v & u\operatorname{cos}v\end{aligned}| \\ & =\operatorname{cos}v\cdot (u\operatorname{cos}v)-(-u\operatorname{sin}v)\cdot \operatorname{sin}v \\ & =u{cos}^{2}v+u{sin}^{2}v \\ & =u({cos}^{2}v+{sin}^{2}v) \\ & =u.\end{aligned}$$

We'll spend some time discussing the meaning behind the Jacobian shortly. But for now, let's get some practice at computing it." :tutorial/id #uuid "f0ea7366-d3d6-5645-99d8-72f7febb8d19" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7668 :tutorial/title "The Jacobian Determinant"} {:db/id 17592186130461 :tutorial/content "To understand what the Jacobian describes, we recall our knowledge of affine transformations.

Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\Bbb R^2 \to \Bbb R^2,$ defined by the matrix equation

$$\mathbf x = T\mathbf u + \mathbf b,$$

where $\mathbf u, \mathbf b,$ and $\mathbf x$ are vectors from $\mathbb R^2,$ and $T$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

For an affine transformation, the determinant of $T$ gives us the following information:

- The *area scale factor* of the transformation:

If a rectangle in the $uv$-plane has area $A,$ its image in the $xy$-plane is a parallelogram of area $|\det(T)|\cdot A.$

![](images/04/04f36d98bf7589d1faadeffee0812590337fd36d8bb44f5abe1920948dee5bb0.png)
- Whether the transformation is *orientation-preserving* or *orientation-reversing:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) > 0,$ the transformation is orientation-preserving.

![](images/49/496a49ee541eab31f69f9c571e450547b0c6942b100bc8e24fbd927dd43e4d33.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) < 0,$ the transformation is orientation-reversing.

![](images/21/211369d6f3fc70bcf7cf40f3270c24c245d306247efc429cb85589e42c19ee07.png)

- Whether the transformation is *invertible* or *non-invertible:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) \neq 0,$ the transformation is invertible.

![](images/e4/e4b840ad5a3efa082ac4056d1d9b7c03d2e3e11e016e053df055dbb2b39f0d1f.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) = 0,$ the transformation is non-invertible. In such cases, a rectangle in the $uv$-plane collapses to either a line segment or point in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/9a/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)

![](images/98/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)

Affine transformations are special because these properties are *global*. In other words, they apply *everywhere* in the plane. So, for example, if $\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage." :tutorial/id #uuid "4dcb1ce1-bfad-524c-a89a-a589532a1067" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7672 :tutorial/title "A Review of Affine Transformations"} {:db/id 17592186130227 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130462 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.

The critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones.

To understand what this means, suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where $$\mathbf{T}: [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] \longrightarrow [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]$$

and we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$

For ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$

$$J(u_0,v_0) = \left.\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}$$

Let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$

![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)

It's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be *approximated* by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson).

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:

- The *local* area scale factor of $\mathbf T$.

Suppose the length and width of our rectangle are $\delta u$ and $\delta v,$ so its area is $\delta A = \delta u\delta v.$ Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the $xy$-plane has an area equal to $\left|J(u_0,v_0)\right| \cdot \delta A.$

![](images/be/be1771ebb041c418c58d7d5615510e2fcacfeaf3677fbace739498ef1998ef11.png)

Note the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced $\det(T)$ with the Jacobian).
- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0)> 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.

![](images/8c/8c649fdd526a831fb990393b292fb4582dad14c2391d129e9ed59792ebb8ac31.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)< 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

![](images/ae/ae5a3d0a42e1c4b9f692994b89815382a30cdf3e676bbd9844258ad2a6961608.png)
- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0)\neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

![](images/33/33ca98206a347e13aa8ec179a52dd755008d9a7d74882391e0c3f2344f6f6641.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

![](images/3d/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)

![](images/65/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)

Points $(u_0,v_0)$ such that $J(u_0,v_0)=0$ are called **critical points.** Critical points are very important. We'll discuss these in more detail in future lessons.

We again stress that the Jacobian describes *local* properties, that is, local to the point $(u_0,v_0).$ The effect of a nonlinear transformation on an object varies as we move around the $uv$-plane, so its local properties also vary. So, for example, if a transformation is orientation-preserving at one point, it does *not* mean it's orientation-preserving everywhere!" :tutorial/id #uuid "3f6a2c63-d9fc-533c-8c4b-fd822216f0f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7673 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind the Jacobian"} :step/id #uuid "0e6a94d3-c32f-5582-98ea-69a8605ef653" :step/math-academy-id 44558 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130230}} {:db/id 17592186130462 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.

:question/math-academy-id "q-161875" :question/problem "Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(0,3)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u-{v}^{2} \\ u+v\end{aligned}]?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡u & -2v \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\cdot 1-1\cdot (-2v) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u+2v \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(0,3)} & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡u+2v)\,{|}_{u=0\,v=3} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡0+2(3) \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|6|\cdot \delta A \\  & =6\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "68b725b2-e4f6-5584-8b86-cedb8363d41b"} {:db/id 17592186406805 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129509 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4471fd6f-9a7d-5e2e-b974-bcbd5ed1ceb0" :question/math-academy-id "q-160601" :question/problem "Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-v \\ 4u-{v}^{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

is (locally) orientation-preserving?" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving at the points where the Jacobian determinant is positive:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}>0.
$$

We have

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-v \\ 4u-{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & -1 \\ 4 & -2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-2v)-4\cdot (-1) \\  & =-4uv+4.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4uv+4 & >0 \\ -4uv & >-4 \\ uv & <1\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Here, we have $x=uv$ and $y=\frac{v}{u}.$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-\frac{v}{{u}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v & u \\ -\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}\, & \frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}| \\  & =v\cdot \frac{1}{u}\text{ }-u\cdot (-\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{2v}{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-2,3)}=\frac{2(3)}{-2}=-3.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡u & -2v \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\cdot 1-1\cdot (-2v) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u+2v \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(0,3)} & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡u+2v)\,{|}_{u=0\,v=3} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡0+2(3) \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|6|\cdot \delta A \\  & =6\,\delta A.\end{aligned}

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡u$ and $y(u,v)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 0 \\ 0 & -3\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\cdot (-3\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-0\cdot 0 \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\pi /4 \\ \pi /4\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4})}=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=3.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "fba89b3b-6b30-58fc-958c-99b3a9d49bb0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406805}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4dc0ac04-220f-5368-899c-f4b853d6caf1" :answer/type {:db/id $$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={v}^{2}+uv$ and $y(u,v)=v-u.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v+u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v & 2v+u \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =v\cdot 1-(2v+u)\cdot (-1) \\  & =v+2v+u \\  & =3v+u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -2\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(8,-2)}=3(-2)+8=2.

$$

$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
