compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={v}^{2}+uv$ and $y(u,v)=v-u.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v+u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v & 2v+u \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =v\cdot 1-(2v+u)\cdot (-1) \\  & =v+2v+u \\  & =3v+u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -2\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(8,-2)}=3(-2)+8=2.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "51873d91-9d02-596a-8782-ed5264ede6c4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186417358}} {:db/id 17592186417358 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281352 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "48838786-15c4-529e-9b61-9a4ae3631e27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/30/3033f0ae73e3f484fc5d3d65e388062feba1824fb3da9971d560cf2f518f49bb.png" :db/id 17592186279238} {:answer/id #uuid "644450bf-23df-5be6-9017-bc23e84a13fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/83/8382e54c1f91ff0e07910c1250c046413814748d9e7ef8968984b7223b43afcc.png" :db/id 17592186279504} {:answer/id #uuid "71de0d63-b9fe-5bf9-98a3-3aa0f0728bad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/fe/fe7bb422a3f992ea88a900e63b2c55df99bce3a785929901c248abadfadf23f1.png" :db/id 17592186279627} {:answer/id #uuid "743bb53f-15e9-5c76-9499-48070c482fc8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/7f/7f214af0b5d71689ec7f21fff043e1779f1d3244c13fdbaf7b8df7f408d66298.png" :db/id 17592186279641} {:answer/id #uuid "9e8384cd-3f08-52be-b19d-6807ce1004b4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/14/14015cadab7d5dc8a9c33d0c1a57a44a79506bd01ba9b1cfe8ec1d280eb3fbb6.png" :db/id 17592186279998}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279504} :answer-field/id #uuid "158dba50-6c99-530b-a3b4-71c1f3ef60c4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280870}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "613ff480-77bb-508e-adea-361b7545c613" :question/math-academy-id "q-161838" :question/problem "Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by

[17592186046658 1007 "Mathematics for Machine Learning" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.
This course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.
On completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.
Students then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.
As part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.

Students also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.
Students work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.
On the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.
Students extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.

$$J(u_0,v_0) = \left.\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}$$

Let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$

![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)

It's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be *approximated* by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson).

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:

- The *local* area scale factor of $\mathbf T$.

Suppose the length and width of our rectangle are $\delta u$ and $\delta v,$ so its area is $\delta A = \delta u\delta v.$ Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the $xy$-plane has an area equal to $\left|J(u_0,v_0)\right| \cdot \delta A.$

![](images/be/be1771ebb041c418c58d7d5615510e2fcacfeaf3677fbace739498ef1998ef11.png)

Note the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced $\det(T)$ with the Jacobian).
- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0)> 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.

![](images/8c/8c649fdd526a831fb990393b292fb4582dad14c2391d129e9ed59792ebb8ac31.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)< 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

![](images/ae/ae5a3d0a42e1c4b9f692994b89815382a30cdf3e676bbd9844258ad2a6961608.png)
- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0)\neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

![](images/33/33ca98206a347e13aa8ec179a52dd755008d9a7d74882391e0c3f2344f6f6641.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

![](images/3d/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)

![](images/65/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)

Points $(u_0,v_0)$ such that $J(u_0,v_0)=0$ are called **critical points.** Critical points are very important. We'll discuss these in more detail in future lessons.

We again stress that the Jacobian describes *local* properties, that is, local to the point $(u_0,v_0).$ The effect of a nonlinear transformation on an object varies as we move around the $uv$-plane, so its local properties also vary.
